P1 Céline’s song is called On ne change pas —”we don’t change.” I think that’s both fortunately and unfortunately true for most of us. Fortunately in the sense that the sweet, innocent, curious, vivacious little one is still inside us, even if hiding. Unfortunate in the sense that we often don’t truly develop the adult qualities that we might pretend to have, so we continue burdening that little one inside us with troubles they aren’t made for handling. This shows up in how we may feel abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.

P2 And I realized that it doesn’t make sense to ask the child to heal itself, which is really a disguised request for the child to abandon its own nature and turn into an adult. There was never anything wrong with the child’s worth to begin with. Instead, we need to separately develop the qualities of a good inner parent for that rightly vulnerable child: the loving Nurturer, safe Protector, and wise Guide.

P4 The Guide is the one people misunderstand the most. I left it out of my first version of this guide until my friend Key pointed it out, and without an inner Guide, it’s easy to go looking for one in a cult. Our lives can become small and like a never-ending therapy session when we focus only on caring for ourselves rather than giving ourselves a mission as well. That’s the Guide’s job. But on the other hand, some people over-rely on their discipline or their mission to avoid caring for themselves.

P7 Sometimes somebody else may have to do one part of the adult role with you or for you first. You get to feel what that is like and watch how they do it.     P1 Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming “shenpa,” and she says “ hooked “ is a more descriptive translation than the usual “attachment.” You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns on you: you’re supposed to be observing yourself. 😀 Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute. You can figure that out later.

    P3 Here’s where I want to clearly depart from the new-age wizdumb that all your problems are self-created: Somebody may really have crossed a boundary. That’s not just because they are your karmic partner mirroring what God wants to show you in yourself, even if that also applies sometimes. Your reaction is what you can control the most, though. If what they did hit something old in you, notice how that feels in your body. And notice how your feelings can also amplify or distort your perceptions of others. Just because your stomach tightened up doesn’t mean their boundary crossing indicates “They’re evil.” You can defer that judgement for when you’re in your happy place.

    P4 Feelings about yourself work the same way. “I feel attracted” or “I feel ashamed” is real as a feeling, but it doesn’t settle who you are, or who you love. Making too much out of something momentary is one side of the human psyche’s pendulum. Give yourself time to see what patterns form more durably, and what feels authentically yours vs something planted or manipulated into being there from society, influencers, family, friends, religion, etc., etc. You may find an exceptional freedom in exactly that in-between place where you don’t have to decide what your pronouns are, or whether you believe in this or that. If you stay in flux forever, though, it can seem like there’s nothing solid about you. In that case, sometimes it helps to meditate or talk with a good unbiased therapist who can help you see the pattern.

    P10 And reaching out doesn’t mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn’t fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller stuff, like whether that thing you told them about your weird fear of birds turns into a joke at the next party 🙈, and how they take it when you say no. (If telling could put you in real danger, like violence, or being outed where that isn’t safe, protect yourself first.) And when someone finally accepts you, it can feel amazing.     Then there’s the stuff that’s hardest to tell anyone, though it’s often exactly what you need help with. Maybe it’s an urge that scares you, or something you did that could get you in legal trouble. (An urge you’ve never acted on isn’t the same as something you did, by the way.) You know that DM you deleted? It can still be sitting on their phone as a screenshot 🙈, and whatever’s on a company’s server can get handed over if a court asks. A fake name doesn’t guarantee you’re anonymous, either. And some of the people you’d tell, like therapists, teachers, and doctors, can be required to report certain things (a few laws cover everybody, too). Which things depends on where you live, and it’s nowhere near every crime you might mention. The cops are hopefully the obvious ones to be careful with, even if they pretend to care.

    P5 Don’t be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself “What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it’s helping?” This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life. Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that’s the endgame, it’s just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy. It’s like real parenting: you might start out reading parenting books and thinking hard about what to say or do, but after a while you get into the groove and a lot of it becomes natural. Inner parenting can be like that too. You don’t need to keep checking this guide or planning every conversation with your little one; the nurturing, protecting and guiding become more automatic. You might still turn to therapy when you need it, and life will keep offering chances to grow wiser and more compassionate. And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn’t as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.

    My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle. Maybe you survived a car crash and surgery a few years ago, but now you’re having trouble with emotional eating. You can draw strength from the past. As my sister, a historian, likes to say, “The past didn’t go anywhere.” Your own challenge doesn’t need to be as dramatic as a car crash, as long as it really happened. So who or what helped you get through it? Is one piece of that still within reach? If you catch yourself thinking “I survived a car crash, so why can’t I stop eating when I’m upset?”, that’s the past turned into a stick to hit yourself with. Maybe you’re more worn out now, or missing whatever helped back then. (No example? Try another doorway.)

    Pema Chödrön calls the tightening and urge you get before the story has finished forming “shenpa,” and she says “ hooked “ is a more descriptive translation than the usual “attachment.” You might notice the hook before you have any clue what part of you is doing the hooking. Or you might notice it embarrassingly late. The jaw and stomach are already tight, and/or half the text is written, and then suddenly it dawns on you: you’re supposed to be observing yourself. 😀 Maybe forget the parts detective work for a minute. You can figure that out later.

    AddedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.
    New insertion — there was no source passage at this position.
    Inner-Child-r03-candidate.html · r0210

    When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: “Oh! I’m hooked again! That’s awesome I could notice it!” If nobody is in danger, take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Sometimes human beings need to be being, not always doing. 🙃 Maybe then you’ll find there’s enough adult around to be nice to your little boo for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you’d regret later.

    AddedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.
    New insertion — there was no source passage at this position.
    Inner-Child-r03-candidate.html · r0211

    Here’s where I want to clearly depart from the new-age wizdumb that all your problems are self-created: Somebody may really have crossed a boundary. That’s not just because they are your karmic partner mirroring what God wants to show you in yourself, even if that also applies sometimes. Your reaction is what you can control the most, though. If what they did hit something old in you, notice how that feels in your body. And notice how your feelings can also amplify or distort your perceptions of others. Just because your stomach tightened up doesn’t mean their boundary crossing indicates “They’re evil.” You can defer that judgement for when you’re in your happy place.

    AddedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.
    New insertion — there was no source passage at this position.
    Inner-Child-r03-candidate.html · r0212

    Feelings about yourself work the same way. “I feel attracted” or “I feel ashamed” is real as a feeling, but it doesn’t settle who you are, or who you love. Making too much out of something momentary is one side of the human psyche’s pendulum. Give yourself time to see what patterns form more durably, and what feels authentically yours vs something planted or manipulated into being there from society, influencers, family, friends, religion, etc., etc. You may find an exceptional freedom in exactly that in-between place where you don’t have to decide what your pronouns are, or whether you believe in this or that. If you stay in flux forever, though, it can seem like there’s nothing solid about you. In that case, sometimes it helps to meditate or talk with a good unbiased therapist who can help you see the pattern.

    AddedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.
    New insertion — there was no source passage at this position.
    Inner-Child-r03-candidate.html · r0213

    The opposite extreme of our pendulum, throwing everything transient away, as some people do with “thought-noting” practice, also isn’t healthy, except as a meditation exercise. Transient feelings and thoughts can be meaningful signals. For example, if you don’t want to be touched, say no now and work out what it means later. Same if something might be dangerous right now, or might be a medical warning sign: step away or get checked first.

Then rest your hands there and notice what you find, no faking required. Non-judgement is a place to start. It can blossom into love over time.

It might just be an inference you’re guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream. Or just nothing comes up, which is also completely OK. Memory is an amorphous thing, easily influenced by guided imagery and suggestions , so we gotta be careful about that. Look at this study, for example , where people were shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took. Half of them actually started sorta remembering it.     P1 I’d look at the parent “script” you inherited: how you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up, long before you started building your Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but it’s often more like a critic, or a warden with rules. The rules can even sound reasonable, like “You can come back to the table when you’re done with your embarrassing crying fit.” If yours was like that, your little one learned bit by bit to hide that part of their authentic self which wasn’t allowed, so they could keep belonging. They might still be doing it.

    P8 Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein came at intuition from two camps of research that were supposed to be at odds, and the paper they wrote together is called Conditions for Intuitive Expertise: A Failure to Disagree . They start from intuition being “sometimes marvelous and sometimes flawed.” Yours too, probably. So which kind is a given hunch? How sure it feels won’t tell you. Their answer, roughly, is to ask whether the situation is predictable at all, and whether you’ve had a real chance to learn it. A hunch can pick up on a pattern before your head can explain it, so hear it out, and then let your head have a look. Neither one should decide alone, though. Your head can get tired of not knowing and be glad to hand the whole thing over, to a hunch or to somebody who sounds sure.

    P1 Two kinds of reaction really are trying to protect you, more often than not. The first one is on duty all the time, and it can sound like a skeptic: “You’re just making this up.” It may have spent years keeping you from being humiliated again, or left again. That’s a long time to stay on guard. It might be tired by now, but it’s experienced and good at what it does. It has probably watched you get excited about other healing things, then drop them.

    Inner-Child-r03-candidate.html · r0271

    Two kinds of reaction really are trying to protect you, more often than not. The first one is on duty all the time, and it can sound like a skeptic: “You’re just making this up.” It may have spent years keeping you from being humiliated again, or left again. That’s a long time to stay on guard. It might be tired by now, but it’s experienced and good at what it does. It has probably watched you get excited about other healing things, then drop them.

    RewrittenReplaces the source passage at this exact position.
    Inner-Child-Humanized-Owner-20261019.html · r0272

    P2 The other one shows up when you get close to something painful, as a sudden pull to do anything but feel it (even a yawn can come with an “I’m so done with this” feeling). It might believe there’s no grown-up around who could hold what’s coming up. I’d want out too. That yawn might actually be the opposite of checking out, though. Re-evaluation Counseling, a kind of peer counseling, counts yawning as emotional discharge, a feeling on its way out. The skeptic and the pull both started out trying to prevent something that really hurt, and they can keep at it even when what they do now hurts you. If you treat either one like an enemy, or like proof that something’s wrong with you, it’ll probably just think “See? I knew it,” and stay in charge. I wonder what it would do if it didn’t have to.

That part tends to step aside once it’s been heard.

    P4 How many tries is enough?     Don’t be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself “What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it’s helping?” This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life. Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that’s the endgame, it’s just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy. It’s like real parenting: you might start out reading parenting books and thinking hard about what to say or do, but after a while you get into the groove and a lot of it becomes natural. Inner parenting can be like that too. You don’t need to keep checking this guide or planning every conversation with your little one; the nurturing, protecting and guiding become more automatic. You might still turn to therapy when you need it, and life will keep offering chances to grow wiser and more compassionate. And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn’t as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.

    Reparenting assumes there’s a clear little one in there to love, and for a lot of people there is. But if you grew up somewhere you only belonged as long as you played somebody else, like a really controlling family or a strict church, the real one may never have had room to form. All this stuff about your little one could have left you wondering who I’m even talking about.

That can make “love yourself” feel pretty empty (love what, when the part you’ve been playing doesn’t feel real?).

    If your childhood meant avoiding pain and keeping the people you needed close, your attention got used up reading danger (was that sigh about me?) and meeting their expectations, and when curiosity or mistakes got you punished, or it felt like they loved you less, you got better at the part. That left much less room for experiments that show you what you like when nobody’s grading you. People grow into who they are by trying things on and then changing their minds, from what they wear down to the ideas and roles they take up, like a teenager who starts spelling her name with an “i” at the end and later changes it back.

It might feel wrong somehow to like something before you’ve checked anyone’s face. You can usually reparent and build who you are at the same time.

You’re after a relationship between them inside you that works better, and that’s hard to have if there’s a new split between an acceptable self and one that has to disappear.

    So early on, the practice is finding out who’s actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader. You might catch yourself explaining who everybody is anyway. Time alone in nature helps too, and so does getting back the preferences that got buried: the foods you really like and what feels good to do, and what you believe and feel when nobody’s around to take your cues from. Focusing (Eugene Gendlin’s method of listening to a vague, felt sense in your body) can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the part you’ve been playing learned to overlook. Any words you put to them can stay tentative (”I hate cooking... or just for everybody?”) while you look at what they seem to mean and revise how you read them.

    Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain.

    AddedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.
    New insertion — there was no source passage at this position.
    Inner-Child-r03-candidate.html · r0301

    Then there’s another bargain, where you have to earn your worth: when you don’t feel your value inside as a human being, you can become a “human doer,” working for it in some arena outside yourself. That might be beauty, athleticism, sexual desirability, intelligence or grades. For some people it’s money or status, and for others it’s a sophisticated spiritual identity or becoming indispensable to everybody else’s problems. It can feel really good to be the one everybody calls. In the more shadowy presentation, when you really need to feel needed, you might be like the firefighters who become arsonists to keep themselves employed.

    AddedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.
    New insertion — there was no source passage at this position.
    Inner-Child-r03-candidate.html · r0302

    Even with good parents, you could have learned unhealthy self-valuation when people repeatedly praised what you did rather than your inherent worth. That wasn’t your flaw. Self-differentiation is learning to notice when you’re making that trade, and to keep your own ground instead.

    Pema Chödrön has a quick map for finding the bargain. It’s four pairs, starting with pleasure and pain, and gain and loss. The other two are about what people think of you: praise and blame, and good reputation and disgrace. Your little one can panic when something hurts, and also when something good might disappear, like praise, romance, money, status, belonging or a spiritual high. You might still be enjoying one of those when your little one starts asking how long this is going to last.

    Differentiation can happen right inside a family, religion, community or relationship. You’d still belong, just selectively. As a differentiated adult you can stay deeply embedded, free to question things or disagree. If a parent used to go quiet and hurt whenever you disagreed, that might be hard to believe. A family where everyone gets to be their own person is healthier than an enmeshed one, and a faith that’s your own is healthier than religious compliance. It can be the same religion either way. And two differentiated people have a sturdier relationship than two who’ve been absorbed into each other.

    I think this is closer to Buddhist practice too. The point is not an impossible performance in which nothing unskillful ever appears. In one discourse (sutta), AN 6.63, the Buddha defines karma in terms of intention (so if you didn’t mean to cause harm, your mind is not poisoned). In DN 2, he explains that in the training to purify the mind, one first recognizes a fault, makes amends, and then restrains themself to prevent that kind of thing in future. So it’s not like, “you’re either pure, or you’re not,” which is where a lot of folks stay stuck. If you’re ashamed about something you chose to do, that might be a signal to give some attention to that. If it’s shame just because of an intrusive thought, then it’s probably not adaptive and can be simply let go of.

    It feels like you’re connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface. What showed me that the daytime pl/ork had stayed shallow was the difference at night. So say you wake up from a dream with far more feeling and need in it than the session came anywhere near. That’s the sign this is you (a session that was good and just didn’t stick around is something else). Then ask what that dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and how you understand it now.     Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt in relationships, and that kind of hurt can only heal so far on your own. Sometimes one person ends up doing a lot of the borrowed grown-up jobs at once. They cook, they keep track of the appointments, they drive, they’re the one who says it’ll be okay, or they’re just the competent person in the room. Maybe you’re picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you’re struggling can be an enormous blessing.

What you’re after is care your little one can count on from more than one place, while the inner relationship stays precious and important. Other jobs can go to friends or community, outsource to the tools or pros, whatever works. You’ll find the balance is dynamic between inner & outer reliance, and going too far in either extreme isn’t generally the healthiest.

    And reaching out doesn’t mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn’t fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller stuff, like whether that thing you told them about your weird fear of birds turns into a joke at the next party 🙈, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you’re still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I’d either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now.     Then there’s the stuff that’s hardest to tell anyone, though it’s often exactly what you need help with. Maybe it’s an urge that scares you, or something you did that could get you in legal trouble. (An urge you’ve never acted on isn’t the same as something you did, by the way.) You know that DM you deleted? It can still be sitting on their phone as a screenshot 🙈, and whatever’s on a company’s server can get handed over if a court asks. A fake name doesn’t guarantee you’re anonymous, either. And some of the people you’d tell, like therapists, teachers, and doctors, can be required to report certain things (a few laws cover everybody, too). Which things depends on where you live, and it’s nowhere near every crime you might mention. The cops are hopefully the obvious ones to be careful with, even if they pretend to care.

    The basic premise of Hearthwork , my peer-counseling framework, is: Equal time. Attention without interpretation, advice, or fixing. You speak. I listen. Then we switch. Presence, Warmth, Discipline, Confidentiality. It’s kind of a third type of relationship, alongside ordinary friendship and professional therapy, and one your little one might really need, because modern life rarely gives you anything like it.

    Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too. When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while. Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time’s up, lends you the Protector. If you say no, they don’t push. But they don’t act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they’re thinking, “Oh, I know what this is about,” or “Here’s what you should do.” They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places, and it’s your turn to keep “Here’s what you should do” to yourself.

    For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule (nobody gets a gold star for forgiving fastest). And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.

    AddedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.

    The understanding that helps me is seeing how a person’s conditioning, history, pain, and capacity shaped the harmful move they made. Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn’t handle. From in there, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through. You may have heard that from somebody telling you to forgive. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you’ve held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

    AddedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.

    Inner-Child-r03-candidate.html · r0406

    They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt. Seeing how they got there doesn’t make it okay. It’s just that punishing them now can’t reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense to see it or the help. Or the skills. What’s left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now. So a boundary can still be right. So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they’d never hear it). Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there. Understanding somebody’s limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential. “I understand how you became this way” can sit right next to “I now understand why I shouldn’t rely on you for this.”

    AddedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.

    Inner-Child-r03-candidate.html · r0407

    Forgiving yourself works the same way. Own what you did (only what was yours), and let yourself feel the remorse. Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends. Changing the behavior counts too. Then you’re allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and the responsibility stays. If you’re thinking “not me, not after what I did,” forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Some harms take years, so don’t push it. Forgive too soon and it’s only a show; stay in the resentment and you end up living there. Every so often, come back to how whoever did it got to be someone who could do that, until you understand it well enough that it changes how you feel.

    Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. So can leaving a family or community, or staying in one on new terms. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo . You don’t have to buy what it teaches about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch where the old you is gone and the new one hasn’t shown up.

    Context

    Paranoia during a rough trip can be a warning sign for psychosis, but it doesn’t automatically lead there, since it can be valid. It tends to go that way when it isn’t balanced by practicality. “The CIA is mind-controlling me!” is paranoia. “The CIA, marketers, and other forces are conspiring to mind-control me, the way they do to everyone else! But since I can see that, I can prevent it to some extent, just by being aware of how it operates” is paranoia too, but it’s practically useful, and less likely to lead to psychosis. “...which means I can prevent it by standing on my head and counting backwards from 33, since 33 is their magic Freemason number!” is leaning psychotic. Some drugs are known for causing paranoia, like THC, so I’d avoid those. If you can’t clearly understand what happened yourself, get someone qualified to help. And if you have an idea of what happened but aren’t sure, ask someone who knows you well.

    Before choosing a therapist, get to know the strengths and pitfalls of their approach, including any modifications they make to the standard protocol. I’d especially want to interview them regarding how they treat spiritual experiences. You want someone who won’t tell you what yours really mean, downplay them, force them, or treat them as a symptom. I’d also want one who doesn’t put ideas in your head, and who understands dissociation. What have they found too challenging to deal with so far, and where have they seen the best results? A good therapist won’t charge you an arm and a leg just for this kind of interview, and they should already have this information on their website to avoid wasting too much time. A certificate on the wall can’t tell you any of that.

    P1 Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain.

    P2 Then there’s another bargain, where you have to earn your worth: when you don’t feel your value inside as a human being, you can become a “human doer,” working for it in some arena outside yourself. That might be beauty, athleticism, sexual desirability, intelligence or grades. For some people it’s money or status, and for others it’s a sophisticated spiritual identity or becoming indispensable to everybody else’s problems. It can feel really good to be the one everybody calls. In the more shadowy presentation, when you really need to feel needed, you might be like the firefighters who become arsonists to keep themselves employed.

    P7 I think this is closer to Buddhist practice too. The point is not an impossible performance in which nothing unskillful ever appears. In one discourse (sutta), AN 6.63, the Buddha defines karma in terms of intention (so if you didn’t mean to cause harm, your mind is not poisoned). In DN 2, he explains that in the training to purify the mind, one first recognizes a fault, makes amends, and then restrains themself to prevent that kind of thing in future. So it’s not like, “you’re either pure, or you’re not,” which is where a lot of folks stay stuck. If you’re ashamed about something you chose to do, that might be a signal to give some attention to that. If it’s shame just because of an intrusive thought, then it’s probably not adaptive and can be simply let go of.

    P1 My father often suggested folks remember a similar-level (or even harder) challenge that they were able to handle.     P1 Maybe you’ve tried picturing your little one and thought, “This feels fake. I’m just making it up.” A real photo of you as a child can help with that, since there’s no face or posture to invent. Yes, yes, it might feel a bit strange, seeing your own face from back then.     Removed — no revised passage occupies this position.

    P2 While you look, notice what your body does and what feelings or urges show up. Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand? Some of it you’ll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then (”You hated that coat”). It might just be an inference you’re guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream. Or just nothing comes up, which is also completely OK. Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.

Memory is an amorphous thing, easily influenced by guided imagery and suggestions, so we gotta be careful about that. Look at this study, for example , where people were shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took. Half of them actually started sorta remembering it. I’m sure you can relate.

    P1 Some people have the opposite problem. It feels like you’re connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface.     P2 The understanding that helps me is seeing how a person’s conditioning, history, pain, and capacity shaped the harmful move they made. Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn’t handle. From in there, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through. You may have heard that from somebody telling you to forgive. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you’ve held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

    Removed — no revised passage occupies this position.
    Structurally removedRemoved from this exact position.
    Inner-Child-Humanized-Owner-20261019.html · r0582

    P3 They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt. Seeing how they got there doesn’t make it okay. It’s just that punishing them now can’t reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense to see it or the help. Or the skills. What’s left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now. So a boundary can still be right. So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they’d never hear it). Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there. Understanding somebody’s limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential. “I understand how you became this way” can sit right next to “I now understand why I shouldn’t rely on you for this.”

    Removed — no revised passage occupies this position.
    Structurally removedRemoved from this exact position.
    Inner-Child-Humanized-Owner-20261019.html · r0583

    P4 Forgiving yourself works the same way. Own what you did (only what was yours), and let yourself feel the remorse. Repair what you can, by apologizing or making amends. Changing the behavior counts too. Then you’re allowed to stop holding yourself hostage, and the responsibility stays. If you’re thinking “not me, not after what I did,” forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Some harms take years, so don’t push it. Forgive too soon and it’s only a show; stay in the resentment and you end up living there. Every so often, come back to how whoever did it got to be someone who could do that, until you understand it well enough that it changes how you feel.

    Removed — no revised passage occupies this position.

    P1 Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. So can leaving a family or community, or staying in one on new terms. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo. You don’t have to buy what it teaches about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch where the old you is gone and the new one hasn’t shown up.

    Removed — no revised passage occupies this position.

    P2 Your little one might be sure everything’s over. Is it? Usually one real thing ended, and there’s other stuff you’re still trying to keep going, maybe on autopilot. Some of it just isn’t known yet, and unknown isn’t the same as gone. Ask your little one what they’re scared will happen in the meantime (worst-case scenarios are kind of their specialty).

    Removed — no revised passage occupies this position.

But you can’t go far with a borrowed coat anyway, so don’t force the future on. Keep taking care of yourself, and grieve what ended with your little one beside you during the metamorphosis.

Or don’t, and just feel the care going their way.

    P1 Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt in relationships, and that kind of hurt can only heal so far on your own. Sometimes one person ends up doing a lot of the borrowed grown-up jobs at once. They cook, they keep track of the appointments, they drive, they’re the one who says it’ll be okay, or they’re just the competent person in the room. Maybe you’re picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you’re struggling can be an enormous blessing.

    P2 Say they’re the one who always remembers your appointments. What you’re after is care your little one can count on from more than one place, while the inner relationship stays precious and important. Other jobs can go to friends or community, outsource to the tools or pros, whatever works. You’ll find the balance is dynamic between inner & outer reliance, and going too far in either extreme isn’t generally the healthiest.

That doesn’t mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but when romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together. It won’t rescue you from the pain or reward you for healing, and it sucks to mess up a beautiful relationship because of unhealed trauma, believe me, I know.     P1 It’s not so hard to understand that words have power. They point your attention somewhere, so aim them at what you want more of, whether that’s something you’d like to be able to do or a relationship. Say you tell yourself “I’m not dependent.” Well, now you’re thinking about being dependent. Being totally independent also isn’t realistic nor ideal, and can even seem like just a reaction to the original problem. We can often strike a nice nuanced poetic balance, like: “I’m provided for by the universe, like the birds & lilies Jesus reminded us of.” With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make it easy to picture: warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, whatever’s really needed to melt into your happy place. You’ll save a ton of money on vacations!

    P6 Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too. When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while. Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time’s up, lends you the Protector. If you say no, they don’t push. But they don’t act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they’re thinking, “Oh, I know what this is about,” or “Here’s what you should do.” They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places, and it’s your turn to keep “Here’s what you should do” to yourself.

I’d also want one who doesn’t put ideas in your head, and who understands dissociation. What have they found too challenging to deal with so far, and where have they seen the best results?     P4 Is a perfect Higher Self already waiting in there to be your guide or parent? I’d call that claim spiritual bypassing . I’ve had the Higher Self perspective myself, though. It’s a somewhat less subjective way of seeing things as working perfectly in reality, despite the ego’s illusions, which matches what people say about it. Where I part ways with IFS is the wisdom part. I don’t think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom. It’s a vantage point, where more wisdom and compassion can come up, but problems can also look like they were never problems at all from up there, and that can ironically lead instead to more foolish indifference. You can see both sides of this see-saw in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self. Anthony de Mello is an excellent example. He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego’s traps and coming back to the Perfect Present. He also had a background as a psychotherapist who understood trauma-informed healing methods. He seemed to drift between the two opposite paradigms in a way that contradicted itself. And that bizarre contradiction is itself cited as “crazy wisdom” by apologists.
